### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Human knowledge and human power meet in one.”

Latin

“Scientia et potentia humana in idem coincidunt.”

Literally “knowledge and human power coincide in the same thing.” The English renders coincidunt as “meet in one,” which keeps the sense of two things arriving at one point.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Knowledge is power.”
-   “Human knowledge and human power meet in one.”

### Attribution notes

Novum Organum I, Aphorism 3. Bacon's aphorism continues: because the cause is unknown, the effect is lost. So he is not coining a slogan about education but stating a condition on action — you cannot produce an effect whose cause you have not found. The English tag “knowledge is power” is a much later and looser reduction of the sentence, and it is not Bacon's wording in any of his works.

#### About Francis Bacon

Francis Bacon (1561–1626) was an English statesman, jurist, and philosopher of inductive science under Elizabeth I and James I. He rose to Lord Chancellor before falling in a bribery scandal.

### Interpretation

Bacon is asserting the principle that would later be called the unity of knowledge and power. His claim in the Novum Organum is that to know a cause is to be able to produce the effect, so ignorance and impotence have the same root. This redirects the aim of inquiry from contemplation to intervention, which is why it marks a break with the earlier tradition. He is careful that the knowledge in question is of causes, not of observed correlations.

#### Why it matters

It sets a demanding test for understanding: if you cannot produce or alter the effect, what you have may be familiarity rather than knowledge.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Human knowledge and human power meet in one.”?

“Human knowledge and human power meet in one.” comes from Novum Organum I, Aph., 3, attributed to Francis Bacon.

#### What does Francis Bacon mean by knowledge?

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, power.

#### Is the wording of this Francis Bacon quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Human knowledge and human power meet in one.” Forms in circulation that differ: Knowledge is power. / Human knowledge and human power meet in one. The Latin reads “Scientia et potentia humana in idem coincidunt.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Novum Organum I, Aphorism 3. Bacon's aphorism continues: because the cause is unknown, the effect is lost. So he is not coining a slogan about education but stating a condition on action — you cannot produce an effect whose cause you have not found. The English tag “knowledge is power” is a much later and looser reduction of the sentence, and it is not Bacon's wording in any of his works.
